## Titanic 

This thrilling PowerPoint is all about a simulated dataset inspired by the titanic dataset in R. <br>
<center>

![](titanic_ship.png){width="4 0 " fig-align="center"}

</center>

The Titanic was famously known for sinking in the Atlantic Ocean during it's voyage from the UK to New York city after hitting an ice berg. The collision with the ice berg resulted in a loss of over half the life's of those on board.(@TitianicInfo)

## The Simulation
The Simulation was done as follows,

renv::init()
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
library(DT)
library(plotly)
library(dplyr)
```

``` r 
# Continuous variable (age)
n <- 1000
age <-  rnorm(n, mean = 35, sd=12) # often recorded discretely but kept continuous here        

# binary variable (sex - 0 = male, 1 = female)
sex <-  rbinom(n, 1, 0.2)   # fewer females

# Define parameters 
beta0 <- -0.5       # Intercept 
beta_sex <- 1.5     # Survival advantage for females
beta_age <- -0.02   # Lower survival for older 


# Linear Predictor
eta <- beta0 +
       beta_sex * sex +
       beta_age * age 

# Simulate binary outcome (assuming survival(i) ~ Bernoulli(pr(i)))
pr <- exp(eta) / ( 1 + exp(eta) )   # Inverse-logit
y = rbinom(n, 1, pr)            # Response variable

# Data set 
titanic <- data.frame(
  Survived = y,
  Sex = sex,
  Age = age
)

# Round age to be a whole number 
titanic <- titanic |> 
 mutate_if(is.numeric, round)
```

```{r}
#| echo:  false
#| cache: true 
#| label: Data simulation
set.seed(200602) # For consistency

# Continuous variable (age)
n <- 1000
age <-  rnorm(n, mean = 35, sd=12) # often recorded discretely but kept continuous here        

# binary variable (sex - 0 = male, 1 = female)
sex <-  rbinom(n, 1, 0.2)   # fewer females

# Define parameters 
beta0 <- -0.5       # Intercept 
beta_sex <- 1.5     # Survival advantage for females
beta_age <- -0.02   # Lower survival for older 


# Linear Predictor
eta <- beta0 +
       beta_sex * sex +
       beta_age * age 

# Simulate binary outcome (assuming survival(i) ~ Bernoulli(pr(i)))
pr <- exp(eta) / ( 1 + exp(eta) )   # Inverse-logit
y = rbinom(n, 1, pr)            # Response variable

# Data set 
titanic <- data.frame(
  Survived = y,
  Sex = sex,
  Age = age
)

titanic <- titanic |> 
 mutate_if(is.numeric, round)

```

## A Deeper Look Into the Dataset 
Here you can look at every "passanger" on the ship and find there sex, age and survival status.

```{r fig.width=2, fig.height=0.2}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
titanic |>
  select(1:3) |>
  datatable(
    options = list(
      pagelength = 10,
      lengthMenu = c(5, 10, 25, 50))
  )
```

## A Deeper Look Into the Dataset
```{r}
plot_ly(
  titanic,
  x = ~Survived,
  y = ~Age,
  type = "box"
)
```

## Some Left Over Tasks

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="45%"}

$$ 
\begin{aligned}
Y &= (X + \beta)^2 \\ 
  &= X^2 + 2X\beta + \beta^2
\end{aligned} 
$$
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}


Lets assume  $\beta = 10$, then we get the following plot,


```{r}
beta <- 10

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(
  data.frame(x = seq(-30, 20, length.out = 200)),
  aes(x, x^2 + 20*x + 100)
) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "X",
    y = "Y"
  )

```
:::
